ego.name: Douglas Engelbart
ego.summary: Douglas Engelbart was an American engineer and computer scientist who developed tools for interactive, collaborative computing. At SRI International, he led the Augmentation Research Center, where his team developed NLS, the computer mouse, hypertext tools, and networked collaboration.

connections.relationship_description: Gladys Charlotte Amelia Munson Engelbart was Douglas Engelbart's mother. She and Carl Louis Engelbart raised their three children in Portland and later near Johnson Creek.
Ballard Fish met Engelbart at Ames Research Center while completing occupational-therapy training. They married on May 5, 1951, and remained married until her death in 1997.
Christina Engelbart was Engelbart's daughter and co-founded the Bootstrap Institute with him in 1988. The institute later became the Doug Engelbart Institute.
connections.notes: Co-founded the Bootstrap Institute with Engelbart in 1988.

connections.relationship_description: Engelbart worked with Hewitt Crane at SRI from 1957 on magnetic devices and electronics miniaturization. They became close friends.
connections.notes: Their work began before Engelbart established the Augmentation Research Center.

connections.relationship_description: Bill English built the first mouse prototype from Engelbart's notes. He also directed key technical elements of the 1968 NLS demonstration.
connections.notes: English was the first person to join Engelbart's Augmentation Research Center in 1964.

connections.relationship_description: Jeff Rulifson led ARC's software team working on NLS. He developed its command language and online editing features and joined the 1968 demonstration.
Carl Louis Engelbart was Engelbart's father. The family moved from Portland to the Johnson Creek countryside when Douglas was eight, and Carl died the following year.
connections.notes: Carl died when Douglas was nine.

connections.relationship_description: Engelbart's older sister; Douglas was the middle child between Dorianne and their younger brother David.
Engelbart's younger brother, born about 14 months after Douglas.
Rowena Swanson supported Engelbart's early SRI research from the Air Force Office of Scientific Research.
connections.notes: Her support helped sustain Engelbart's early SRI research.

connections.relationship_description: Robert Taylor directed NASA funding to Engelbart's computer-display research at SRI. That support contributed to work leading to the mouse.
connections.notes: Taylor also attended the 1968 NLS demonstration.

connections.relationship_description: SRI management placed the remaining ARC staff under Bertram Raphael in 1976. He negotiated ARC's transfer to Tymshare.
connections.notes: The transfer moved ARC and its NLS software to Tymshare.

connections.relationship_description: Bill Paxton was an ARC associate who joined the 1968 demonstration remotely from Menlo Park. He collaborated with Engelbart and Rulifson during the live presentation.
Stewart Brand advised Engelbart and the ARC team on presenting the 1968 demonstration. He also operated a camera from Menlo Park during the event.
connections.notes: Supported the production of the 1968 demonstration.

category_summaries.summary: Engelbart's family connected the private commitments of his early life with the institutions of his later work. He married Ballard Fish while defining his career purpose, and their daughter Christina joined him in founding the Bootstrap Institute in 1988.

Engelbart's professional circle gave him research support and organizational settings for his work. At SRI, collaborators and funders helped develop his augmentation program. SRI management later transferred ARC to Tymshare, where limited funding and interest constrained further development.

ARC turned Engelbart's ideas about collective work into NLS. Its engineers and programmers developed the mouse, display interaction, hypertext, shared editing, and remote communication. The team presented the system in San Francisco in 1968.
Stewart Brand helped the ARC team prepare the 1968 demonstration for a conference audience. His presentation advice and camera work supported the live connection between San Francisco and Menlo Park.
